candidates.text:
𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗼𝗻 𝗧𝗮𝗽. 𝗦𝘇𝗻 𝟬𝟯. 𝗩𝗼𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴
12 of us spent an afternoon at the minimi villa in Indiranagar working through one question: what does it take for a voice agent (an AI you phone up and talk to) to answer in half a second?

Anyone running a voice agent cares about three things: delay (how long the caller waits after they stop talking), quality (did it hear, understand and answer well) and cost per minute. Almost every decision helps one and hurts another.

The room didn't agree on which matters most. Some use cases want a reply now and will forgive a weaker answer. Others will wait a second or two but can't afford a wrong one. One person's experience was that callers care more about delay than quality: if the agent takes 5 seconds, the answer had better be extraordinary. And voice has a floor that chat doesn't. Go silent for 6-7 seconds on a call and the caller starts saying "hello? are you there?"

So we split the three into one goal and a set of limits, the same way you'd frame a project at work this quarter.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗚𝗼𝗮𝗹 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗟𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘁𝘀
The goal was 500ms for TTFA. A natural conversation sits at about 500–800 ms, and 500 was the number the room called golden.

Cost had to stay under ₹2 a minute. People quoted ₹1–3 a minute for systems running today, with ₹1.5 as the number to beat. The LLM and text-to-speech are where most of that money goes.

The hardware stays fixed. A faster GPU reads faster, and if you pack proportionally more callers onto it, cost per minute stays flat. But that scaling is rarely linear, and it was one variable too many for an afternoon.

Quality can't drop, so only lossless tricks were allowed. Anything that might change the model's answers, like quantization (storing the model's numbers with fewer bits), was off the table. One line settled the debate: from the inference side, speed is the only part of quality you touch. How good the answer is belongs to the LLM/model. We're purely focused on inference.

Tool calls were parked for the first pass, because the time they add is too unpredictable to reason about. We came back to them at the end.

Then we mapped out general times across a voice ai inference stack. we also agreed to count only blocking time. since a lot of the work can be parallelized, but some times are just purely blocking.

our rough blocking times:

network: 50 ms

On turn: 500–800 ms
STT: 200–300 ms
LLM: 0.3–1.5 s
TTS: 200–300 ms
Network: 50 ms
this adds up to 1.3–3 seconds, against a goal of 0.5.

we then went stack by stack

solving with either two ways
1. you bring real world implementation someone has done and gotten results for

2. research papers anyone has read that tackles this skillfully.

And we started 👇🏻

𝟭 · 𝗪𝗮𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼 𝗕𝗲 𝗦𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆'𝘃𝗲 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗲𝗱 (𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗻𝗲𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺)

There are two ways to tell that someone has stopped. Listening to the sound is fast, about 80–100 ms, because people tend to trail off before they stop. But it hears "I want to order a burger from…" followed by a pause and decides the turn is over. Reading the words catches that, but it has to wait for the transcript, so it's four to five times slower.

Where we agreed: use the sound as the fast first filter, and when it thinks the caller has stopped, check the last few words before committing. That makes the sound check a dial for how many false alarms you'll accept.

The best idea in the room was to set that dial per use case rather than per person. A support call and a career counselling call need different patience, and a therapy call can't keep cutting people off. You know the use case before the call starts, so the setting costs no time.

𝟮 · 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗕𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗵

The idea is to stream the half-finished transcript into the LLM, so it has already read most of the sentence by the time the caller stops.

One person had built exactly this and dropped it. Speech-to-text keeps revising earlier words as more audio arrives, and every revision throws away reading the GPU has already done.

Another person had a fix: only pass on words that stayed the same across two transcript updates in a row. If "book a table for" survives when the next word arrives, it's safe to send. That cut re-reading to 14% of the time.

It works because a voice agent's input only ever grows. The instructions stay fixed, and each new turn is added to the end. Trade: the earlier you start, the more delay you save and the more GPU work you risk wasting.

𝟯 · 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗟𝗟𝗠: 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗪𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴

One caller on one GPU is easy. The real problem is keeping that speed when a hundred callers share the GPU. The two biggest levers that don't change the model's output are the KV cache (the notebook the model keeps of everything it has already read, so it never reads it twice) and scheduling (deciding whose work runs next).

Voice has one useful quirk. Writing speed barely matters, because people speak much slower than a model writes, so a scheduler can push a new caller's first few tokens ahead of everything else on the GPU.

Another lever is doing the reading and the writing on separate machines. The worry is the time it takes to ship notebooks between them, but one person who had run this on a three-machine cluster said it didn't matter: the machines sat in the same rack on a very fast link.

𝟰 · 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗖𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗮𝘁 𝗢𝗻𝗰𝗲

The real problem at scale is routing. A call arrives in turns with gaps in between, and a normal load balancer sends each turn to whichever machine is free. That machine doesn't have the notebook, so it re-reads the whole conversation. The fix: send every turn of a call back to the machine that already holds its notebook, with sticky sessions or by routing on a fingerprint of the conversation so far.

𝟱 · 𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝗖𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘀

A tool call (the model looking something up) will never fit in 500 ms. Say something first, because "let me check that" is what a person would say too. And fetch before you're asked: on a support call the caller will probably ask about their orders, so pull that data when the call starts.

I had such a blast today. Happy weekending everyone!

candidates.text:
The return on time is going higher and higher. 

One of the signs that you are embracing AI is that you have less time than before, because you have more work. 

So, Which world are we in?

(A) There is a one-time digestion phase where AI consumes times as workflow adapt

(B) The opp’y cost of not using AI is such that there is no foreseeable rate limiting dininshing return to using AI as it improves

Intuitively, most people will think (A). 

But, if you are pushing hard, the answer is (B). 

All these AI tools will need to be re-factored. 

Execution was once a serial. Now you can run parallel paths. 

The opportunity cost of AI is so high, that before going to bed, you should prompt AI to build something overnight. 

Founders that have endurance are going to crush lifestyle Founders. 

(Aside: The higher return on time is consistent with greater productivity growth, higher returns on capital, and higher long-run interest rates.)
